=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine ===

[Source 1 — kyivindependent.com (Bias: Independent / Unrated)] (URL: https://kyivindependent.com/democrats-poised-to-sweep-us-congress-in-midterms-delivering-setback-to-trump/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine

The Associated Press projected that Democrats had won control of the Senate, while NBC News projected a Democratic victory in the House of Representatives. Vote counting remained underway in several congressional races.

Actual Article Body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.

Democrats are projected to take control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, dealing a major setback to President Donald Trump.The Associated Press projected that Democrats had won control of the Senate, while NBC News projected a Democratic victory in the House of Representatives. Vote counting was still underway in several congressional races.

Trump told the New York Times he is "absolutely willing" to accept the results, as he is set to spend his remaining two years in office dealing with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

The midterm election, widely seen as a referendum on the sitting president's performance, was defined by concerns over the cost of living, rising fuel prices, and the war with Iran.

The Democratic gains could also have consequences for U.S. foreign policy.

Democratic lawmakers have vowed to rein in Trump's approach to Russia, Ukraine, and the Middle East, potentially creating more pressure on the administration to maintain support for Kyiv and take a tougher line toward Moscow.

The election comes at a low point in U.S.-Ukraine relations.

Trump has faced criticism from U.S. lawmakers, Kyiv, and European capitals for allowing Russian diesel into the U.S. and easing sanctions on Russia — moves that critics say undermine the West's strategy for ending the war.

Several Senate races were particularly important for Kyiv, including contests in Texas, Kansas, and Michigan, where candidates held differing positions on Ukraine.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, flipping the seat for Democrats. Paxton had defeated longtime pro-Ukraine Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary after attacking Cornyn's support for Ukraine aid and related measures, including efforts involving seized Russian assets.

Paxton campaigned on an "America First" platform and opposed what he called "blank checks" for foreign countries. Talarico, by contrast, explicitly supports helping Ukraine.

Democrat @jamestalarico wins Texas's U.S. Senate race, defeating Republican @KenPaxtonTX. https://t.co/wtms326N4X

Kansas also flipped to Democrats, with Adam Hamilton defeating Republican Roger Marshall. Marshall has opposed major Ukraine aid packages, describing them as unpaid "blank checks," and has prioritized domestic spending. More recently, he aligned himself with Trump's position by blaming the war in Ukraine for high diesel prices.

Hamilton criticized Marshall's position during debates, accusing him of selling out Ukraine. He has voiced support for Kyiv and opposed deals involving Russian diesel.

The race was unexpectedly competitive in a deeply Republican state.

Democrat Adam Hamilton @Hamilton4Kansas is running for U.S. Senate in Kansas [KS-Sen] on November 3.
✅Supports humanitarian aid
✅Condemns U.S. abandonment of Ukraine
✅Condemns Russian invasion
✅Pro-Ukrainian rhetoric https://t.co/8g0o2PUBc8

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was defeating Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed supports assistance to Ukraine, while Rogers has taken a more cautious position.

Rogers said he would have supported a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill that Trump later waived. He has also said he does not want to give Russian President Vladimir Putin "an inch" and has rejected claims that Trump is siding with Russia.

The shift toward a Democratic majority in the Senate could mean more lawmakers who reliably support aid to Ukraine.

But the change does not guarantee that Congress will be able to overcome opposition from the White House or Republican lawmakers.

In the House of Representatives, Ukrainian-born Republican Congresswoman Victoria Spartz lost her reelection bid in Indiana's 5th Congressional District.

Spartz has been a vocal critic of President Volodymyr Zelensky and U.S. military assistance to Kyiv.

Republican Representative Anna Paulina Luna, who has spread pro-Russian narratives and invited sanctioned Russian lawmakers to visit the U.S., was projected to retain her seat after Democrat Leela Gray, a retired Army brigadier general, lost the race.

Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a leader of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus and one of Ukraine's staunchest supporters in Congress, has lost his reelection bid.

If Democrats take control of the House, they could also change which Ukraine-related bills receive votes and how closely the Trump administration's policies are scrutinized.

Should House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries replace Mike Johnson as speaker, Republican lawmakers skeptical of aid to Ukraine would lose their ability to block pro-Ukraine legislation from reaching the floor.

Democrats could also use their oversight powers to investigate SpaceX founder Elon Musk, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Trump's peace envoys, experts previously told the Kyiv Independent.

Musk is allegedly responsible for the temporary throttling of Starlink services in Ukraine, Hegseth is said to be delaying shipments of Patriot missiles, and the U.S. peace envoys have faced scrutiny for at times pushing peace deals favorable to Moscow.

Despite the projected gains, Democrats will face significant obstacles to passing legislation that Trump opposes.

Even after securing the 51 Senate seats needed for a simple majority, they would still need Republican support to overcome the filibuster — a Senate procedure that generally requires 60 votes to advance major legislation.

The Senate has previously demonstrated that bipartisan support for Ukraine remains possible. In August, lawmakers passed the Lindsey Graham Act, a Russia sanctions bill spearheaded by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, with 86 votes.

But that consensus cannot be taken for granted, particularly when Republican lawmakers face pressure to support Trump's agenda.

Even if Democrats secure enough votes to pass legislation providing assistance to Ukraine or imposing tougher sanctions on Russia, Trump could veto it.

Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers of Congress, a threshold Democrats are unlikely to reach on their own.

One alternative would be to attach Ukraine-related provisions to legislation Congress must pass, including defense spending bills and the National Defense Authorization Act.

These measures could give Democrats more influence over U.S. policy toward Ukraine, though Trump's veto power limits their ability to challenge the administration.

Reporter

News Editor, North America

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Democrats cap off midterm night to remember as they clinch 218 seats to win House to go with Senate sweep

Democrats are projected to retake the House majority in the 120th Congress, ending Republicans‘ trifecta in Washington to cap a night in which they sailed to victory in both chambers of Congress. The magic number of 218 seats was obtained in the early hours of Wednesday morning, according to the Associated Press, with Johnny Garcia […]

Actual Article Body:
Democrats are projected to retake the House majority in the 120th Congress, ending Republicans‘ trifecta in Washington to cap a night in which they sailed to victory in both chambers of Congress.

The magic number of 218 seats was obtained in the early hours of Wednesday morning, according to the Associated Press, with Johnny Garcia winning Texas’s 35th District, adding salt to the GOP’s wound as the seat was redrawn to try to guarantee a Republican victory during the 2025 redistricting frenzy.

The result was the cherry on top of a congressional sundae, after they secured a dominant victory in the Senate, with at least 54 seats.

The victory gives Democrats a foothold in Washington after they lost both chambers of Congress and the White House in the 2024 elections. For Republicans, the flipping of the House chambers throws GOP leadership into uncertainty and means President Donald Trump‘s agenda in his final two years in power will likely be stymied if not totally derailed. Trump himself told Fox News that he had already spoken with Democrats, although did not elaborate who he spoke to or what he spoke about.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) is expected to take the speaker’s gavel in the next session of Congress, but his path to doing so may be complicated by his incoming freshman class, which contains several socialist and progressive members who are reportedly angling for concessions in exchange for their support. Centrist-aligned Democrats also carried several districts across the Midwest and South.

“The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” Jeffries said at a press conference Tuesday night. “They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January. We understand, as House Democrats, that life is way too expensive in this great country of ours.”

Jeffries was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries,” and those at his election night watch party roared when he took the stage, hours after the drinks flowed from the open bar amid an energetic crowd of activists and staff.

Democrats have signaled that they intend to exercise their oversight authority over the Trump administration over the next two years, with plans to investigate Trump’s family’s business dealings, immigration enforcement tactics, the Epstein files, and more. In a sign of how difficult the president may find things, now-House oversight committee ranking member Robert Garcia (D-CA) advised the president to “LAWYER UP.”

BLUE WAVE CARRIES SENATE DEMOCRATS BACK INTO POWER FOR FINAL YEARS OF TRUMP PRESIDENCY

It remains to be seen whether Democrats will try to impeach Trump once again with their newfound majority. Democrats have been hesitant to pursue impeachment action against Trump, believing such a move may play in the president’s favor. Some Democrats have been outspoken in their support of impeaching members of the Cabinet, such as War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Still, Jeffries said Democrats “haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out” when asked about impeachment.

Lauren Green contributed to this report.

Trump reacts to Republican losses and declines to take blame | CNN Politics

By the time the House and Senate had been called for Democrats on Tuesday, a consensus among members of both parties was forming: voters had rejected President Donald Trump’s record in office, and he would face a starkly different political reality for the remainder of his term.

Actual Article Body:
By the time the House and Senate had been called for Democrats on Tuesday, a consensus among members of both parties was forming: voters had rejected President Donald Trump’s record in office, and he would face a starkly different political reality for the remainder of his term.

Trump, however, sees it very differently.

“But I don’t view it as a hit on me,” Trump told Fox News in a live phone interview. “We’ve had the greatest two years in the history of the presidency in terms of the economy, in terms of all the things that we’ve done.”

The stunning results across a swath of America were not primarily the fault of the Iran war he began eight months ago — he told the Wall Street Journal that was only a “piece” of it — or the tariffs that drove up prices or his fixation on topics far from voters’ minds, Trump insisted.

It was the candidates who were to blame, he argued, helped along by favorable coverage of Democrats on his once-favorite channel, Fox News. The results were only a “little surprise,” he would later tell that channel. The winds of history were always against him, he’d long warned. He neglected to mention that he had selected many of the candidates himself.

“I thought they’d do better,” he told Fox, referring to Republicans in the third person rather than the party he is currently leading. Later, he attributed the losses to a “mood in the air.”

He also insisted Tuesday night that his governing agenda would continue apace, despite the dramatically altered political conditions in Washington.

The election results were the punctuation on a long and often frustrating campaign season for Trump, who spent the bulk of the last month flying aboard Air Force One to red states with the task of encouraging supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

The gambit did not work, but Trump saw fault not in his own performance but in that of the people he was trying to help.

“They just didn’t inspire the people to get out and vote,” he told Fox. “And I wasn’t on the ballot. If I was on the ballot, they would have got out.”

Many of the candidates who lost on Tuesday — including Darline Graham in South Carolina, Ken Paxton in Texas, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Mike Collins in Georgia — were hand-selected by Trump himself, in some cases over the objections of other Republicans.

He did not mention that as he bemoaned the candidates’ inability to translate his support into votes.

“I had no choice,” he said of the decision to support Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued candidate in Texas he endorsed over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. “When it wasn’t fashionable, he kissed my ass.”

How intensively Trump wanted to pin blame on his party’s candidates seemed to vary by the minute.

“I’m going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!” he wrote, ominously, on Truth Social a few minutes before midnight.

His first target was Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, the Republican incumbent who lost re-election to Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Trump deemed him a “Republican in name only” and claimed “He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!”

But in a phone interview with Politico around the same time, he insisted he wasn’t interested in assigning blame.

“I don’t want to blame anybody,” he said. “I just want to say, you know, it was a very interesting period of time. I watched with great interest, learned from it.”

Trump sounded more conciliatory toward Democrats, who he will now be forced to rely upon if he wants to pass anything through Congress. He made similar pledges after Republicans lost the House in the 2018 midterms, but the offers of bipartisanship did not materialize.

“You know, I have a lot of friends that are Democrats. Believe it or not, I’ve already spoken to some of them,” he said, without naming them.

He spoke vaguely of trying to find areas of compromise, but insisted he had no regrets about the issue many Republicans blame most for Republicans’ woes — the war in Iran.

“I don’t think about it. I did the right thing,” he told the Wall Street Journal when asked if he had regrets about the war. “I would have done it again.”

“I had no choice,” he said of the decision to support Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued candidate in Texas he endorsed over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. “When it wasn’t fashionable, he kissed my ass.”

How intensively Trump wanted to pin blame on his party’s candidates seemed to vary by the minute.

“I’m going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!” he wrote, ominously, on Truth Social a few minutes before midnight.

His first target was Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, the Republican incumbent who lost re-election to Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Trump deemed him a “Republican in name only” and claimed “He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!”

But in a phone interview with Politico around the same time, he insisted he wasn’t interested in assigning blame.

“I don’t want to blame anybody,” he said. “I just want to say, you know, it was a very interesting period of time. I watched with great interest, learned from it.”

Trump sounded more conciliatory toward Democrats, who he will now be forced to rely upon if he wants to pass anything through Congress. He made similar pledges after Republicans lost the House in the 2018 midterms, but the offers of bipartisanship did not materialize.

“You know, I have a lot of friends that are Democrats. Believe it or not, I’ve already spoken to some of them,” he said, without naming them.

He spoke vaguely of trying to find areas of compromise, but insisted he had no regrets about the issue many Republicans blame most for Republicans’ woes — the war in Iran.

“I don’t think about it. I did the right thing,” he told the Wall Street Journal when asked if he had regrets about the war. “I would have done it again.”
